answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Whether or not a separate impact metric is developed and made available to reporting organizations, it is still critical that the inventory market-based scope 2 method adopt the proposed changes.

An impact metric cannot offer the same true decarbonization signals & incentives on every grid in which organizations operate, as it is a fundamentally different question of estimating how one action in one time & place changes the world compared to an unobserved counterfactual. Effectively, it is similar in nature to carbon offsetting rather than being an approach aligned with power market & grid fundamentals. This is then compared to other actions in another place & time. There is missing alignment between these actions which do not drive true deep decarbonization of the grid.

The impact metric must meet the following criteria to be useful & trustworthy as an estimate of avoided & induced emissions as intended:

Additionality:
- Impact metrics allow for a comparison between emissions induced by electricity usage on one grid with emissions avoided by actions taken on another grid at another time. In this kind of dynamic, it is essential that the action being taken to reduce emissions elsewhere is evaluated with strict additionality tests.

Transparent methods:
- The methodology rests on estimating emissions that are being compared to a counterfactual world. This means there will always be uncertainty. The formulas & models used to make these emissions estimations must be transparent & repeatedly publicly reviewed for accuracy to ensure public trust & usefulness to companies.

Continued clarity this metric is fully separate from inventory accounting:
- MBM inventory accounting is distinctly different from an impact metric, & the two should remain separated for reporting purposes. The GHGP has made it clear these processes will be unaffected by the other & the use of these methodologies in any target-setting or regulatory instance is not for GHGP to decide.

EnergyTag does not believe investments made outside of time-matched & deliverable procurements are inherently something to oppose, as long as Scope 2 inventory accounting progresses in line with proposed updates. However, that does not mean EnergyTag is not concerned with the validity & transparency around proposed impact metrics. More quality engagement & development is necessary to make this a useful element of clean energy procurement moving forward.

To date, there hasn’t been a proposed impact methodology that satisfactorily meets the combined GHGP metrics of integrity, impact, & feasibility:

“Short-run Marginal Emission Rates Omit Important Impacts Of Electric-sector Interventions”:
https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119

TU Berlin study: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.11377
"MCI (Marginal Carbon Intensity), despite its conceptual appeal, does neither capture the needs of carbon-aware approaches focused on reducing Scope 2 emissions (a clear, transparent, and verifiable methodology) nor of efforts to optimize grid efficiency."

“From Power Markets to Reality: Does the Marginal Power Plant Really Exist?”: https://www.electricitymaps.com/content/from-power-markets-to-reality-does-the-marginal-power-plant-really-exist

NRDC: https://www.nrdc.org/bio/pete-budden/once-generation-chance-fix-corporate-emissions-reporting

Finally, EnergyTag also notes the serious reputational risks posed to the GHGP, WRI, etc. if offsetting-type schemes like impact accounting are not rigorously & transparently defined, audited, & implemented.
Financial Times exposure:
https://www.ft.com/content/2d6fc319-2165-42fb-8de1-0edf1d765be3?sharetype=blocked

Given there is currently little agreement on impact metric methods or quality evidence to support any given method’s long-term consequential impacts & efficacy, EnergyTag encourages GHGP to ensure sufficient time to develop a high integrity approach based on transparent & concrete methodologies.

answers.label: Why annual or lifetime reporting
answers.text:
It does not make sense for projects falling under consequential accounting to be reported with inherently uncertain, decades-out modeling when inventory and other reporting must be done using verifiable historical data each year.

“The Once in a Generation Chance to Fix Corporate Emissions Reporting”: https://www.nrdc.org/bio/pete-budden/once-generation-chance-fix-corporate-emissions-reporting

Any consequential accounting method must be held to this integrity standard of robust yearly calculation of claimed impacts, using the most transparent, repeatable, accurate, and auditable methodologies and data sources.

“From Power Markets to Reality: Does the Marginal Power Plant Really Exist?”: https://www.electricitymaps.com/content/from-power-markets-to-reality-does-the-marginal-power-plant-really-exist
“Moving Beyond Marginal Carbon Intensity: A Poor Metric for Both Carbon Accounting and Grid Flexibility” (TU Berlin): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.11377

This is especially true considering the rapidity with which perceived primary impacts (let alone secondary impacts) can change, especially those modeled over timescales as large as the entire lifetime of a project.

“Short-run Marginal Emission Rates Omit Important Impacts Of Electric-sector Interventions”:
https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2211624119
